sections.html:
The office is open to the public on weekdays, opening at eight and closing at half past four. The office page carries a Location Directions link for the street address. Every deed, mortgage and discharge touching Lapeer County land is filed there, and staff promise prompt handling of papers that satisfy the Michigan Recording Act.

Payment can be cash, a check or money order made out to Lapeer County Register of Deeds, or a card used at the counter itself. Title companies and attorneys who file in volume are pointed to Simplifile for electronic submission, and that vendor's help line is 800.460.5657.

A homeowner bringing in a deed should have it signed in dark ink, with each signer's name printed or stamped under the signature, the buyer's street address shown, and the drafter's name and business address on the page.

The flat charge is $30 for each document, however long it runs. A sale adds transfer tax and, for most warranty forms, a tax certificate. The office posts every figure on one fee sheet.

sections.h2: Deeds the treasurer must certify first
sections.html:
The fee sheet singles out warranty deeds, land contracts, land contract assignments and any deed containing a covenant of warranty. The County Treasurer has to certify each one ahead of recording.

The certificate costs $5, so allow time for that stop before the recording counter. If your paper is some other kind of instrument, ask the treasurer's office whether it also requires one. If the parcel carries unpaid back taxes, talk with the treasurer about what must be cleared before a certificate is issued.

Combined, the two rates come to $8.60 for every thousand dollars of value, and the seller pays at recording. The instrument must show the full value of the land and buildings, or carry an attached affidavit that gives it. MCL 207.504 writes the county rate as 55 cents per $500 or fraction, which is the same as the $1.10 per thousand on the local sheet.

The Transfer Tax page on the county site links two exemption lists. The county statute, MCL 207.505, excuses several kinds of paper:

  • anything where the money involved is under $100;
  • a mortgage or other security paper, and its later assignment or release;
  • leases, plus land contracts while legal title stays with the seller;
  • a spouse to spouse conveyance that sets up or ends ownership by the entireties;
  • a quitclaim that merely fixes a defect in a title already held;
  • a court order moving title with no dollar amount attached.

Nothing changes on the tax bill automatically. The County Treasurer cannot take a name off a bill, so the new owner or the seller has to carry the deed or other proof of transfer to the assessor in the township, city or village where the property lies.

Until the assessor updates the record, the old name may keep receiving the July 1 and December 1 bills from the local treasurer. A bill that goes unpaid after March 1 moves to the county as delinquent, with the 4% administration fee and interest attached, so buyers and sellers should settle who is watching the mailbox before the closing date. Mortgage lenders sometimes miss a payment, and the owner remains responsible for confirming the bill was paid.

sections.h2: Recording a deed step by step
sections.html:
Start with the deed type. A warranty deed, a land contract or any paper with a covenant of warranty goes to the County Treasurer first for the $5 certification. If taxes are open, settle them before that stop.

Next, check the paper against the formatting list below, and make sure the full value appears on the deed or an affidavit is attached. Write any exemption on the face of the deed. Then bring it to the Register of Deeds with the $30 recording charge and the transfer tax. Most sellers skip all of this and let the title company file, which is the simplest route if a lender or an escrow is involved.

After recording, remind the new owner to take proof of transfer to the local assessor so the next bill carries the right name.

sections.h2: Why a deed gets turned away
sections.html:
A register may not receive a paper that skips the formatting rules in MCL 565.201. The usual causes are small and fixable before you arrive.

  • A printed name that differs from the name in the notary's acknowledgment.
  • Pages with too little white space: the first page needs about two and a half inches clear at the top.
  • Type under 10-point, or ink that is not black on white stock.
  • Full Social Security numbers left visible, when only the last four digits may show.
  • No English translation attached to a foreign-language document.
  • A first line that fails to name the one recordable event the paper evidences.

Once a paper is accepted, the law presumes it complies, and a register cannot reject a conforming instrument because of its content.

MCL 600.2567 allows extras that the Lapeer sheet does not itemize. A name search can be billed at fifty cents for each year covered, with a $5 floor, and any other filing or lookup is $1 per paper.

  • $5 of each $30 recording fee is set aside for the county's automation fund.
  • The statute counts a page as one side of a sheet 8.5 inches wide and 11 to 14 inches long.
  • Foreclosure deeds and forfeiture certificates that a treasurer files can be settled after the sale on a delayed schedule instead of at the counter.

Phone the office before a research trip and ask how a search request would be priced.

Enroll in the free email alert the office offers. Every filing made in a name you list sends a message, so a forged deed or loan against your house gets noticed early.

The signup is announced at the top of the office page, and a one page form sits on the county website. Sellers should also confirm that the name on their title matches the name they plan to sign, because a mismatch with the acknowledgment is one of the statute's own grounds for refusal.

Lapeer County is more rural than Oakland County next door, and many parcels are farms or lake lots. A seller with an older family property should look up the recorded chain of title early, so any gap or name mismatch is found before a buyer finds it.

faqs.q: What is the filing fee for a deed in Lapeer County?
faqs.a: Thirty dollars per document, however many pages. A warranty deed adds a $5 certificate from the County Treasurer, and the seller owes transfer tax at $1.10 plus $7.50 for every thousand dollars of value.
Monday to Friday, opening at eight and closing at half past four. The Location Directions link on the office page gives the street address.
Yes, at the counter only. The office also takes cash, checks and money orders, and checks are written to Lapeer County Register of Deeds.

faqs.q: Who covers transfer tax in a Lapeer County sale?
faqs.a: The seller. The deed shows the total value or has a valuation affidavit attached, and the exemptions under MCL 207.505 apply to the county portion.

faqs.q: Can I be warned if someone records a deed in my name?
faqs.a: Yes. The office runs a free email service that alerts you to any filing under a name you enter.
